explanations.answer: The Jews overpower those who hated them
explanations.explanation: That's the flip, friend. The text says the enemies had hoped to overpower the Jews, but “…their plan was overturned and the Jews overpowered those who hated them.” (Esther 9:1) You ever plan your whole day down to the minute, and the day shows up with its own ideas? Same energy, except this was a much bigger deal.

explanations.answer: The enemies win the day without a fight
explanations.explanation: Close, but the verse says the enemies only hoped to overpower the Jews. Hoping is not winning, baker. I've hoped a cookie would cool itself the second it left the oven, and my fingers have the receipts. The text says their plan was overturned (Esther 9:1).

explanations.answer: The king calls the whole day off
explanations.explanation: Nobody calls this day off. The text says it was the day the king's command and edict were to be executed, and the day went forward. The plan that got overturned was the enemies' plan, not the king's. Once that edict was out, it was on the calendar, like a batch already in the oven.
Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite: “No man could withstand them…” (Esther 9:2). Not plenty of men, not a few, not one. That's a full empty line of folks who couldn't hold their ground.

Right, it's false. The text says, “No man could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen upon all peoples.” (Esther 9:2) Zero men able to stand against them. Zero! If I had a cookie box with that kind of zero, I'd be in trouble.

explanations.answer: The fear of them has fallen on all peoples
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse gives the reason itself: “…because the fear of them had fallen upon all peoples.” (Esther 9:2) That's the only reason it gives, so I'll stop there. Sometimes the best thing a verse does is just tell you.

explanations.answer: The king's own army stands guard over them
explanations.explanation: I'd love to tell you about a big army standing guard, but the text never mentions one here. It says the Jews assembled in their cities, and that the fear of them had fallen on all peoples (Esther 9:2). I'm not adding soldiers the passage doesn't hand me. That's how cookie recipes get ruined, friend.

explanations.answer: Their enemies have all fled the provinces
explanations.explanation: Nobody fled in this verse. It says the Jews assembled to attack those who sought to harm them, so those folks were still there. The reason no one could withstand them is that the fear of them had fallen on all peoples (Esther 9:2).

They did. The text lists them all: the officials, the satraps, the governors, and the king's administrators, and says they “helped the Jews” (Esther 9:3). That's a whole government lineup on one side. I've never had that many folks helping with one batch, and I once had a very good week.
Staying out would be the easy choice, but that's not what the text says. It says all of them “helped the Jews” (Esther 9:3). Nobody sat this one out and watched from the sidelines.

Other way around, friend. The officials, satraps, governors and administrators helped the Jews (Esther 9:3). It's a surprising turn after the enemies' plan. The side the enemies hoped would back them ended up helping the other team.

Mordecai, Queen Esther's cousin, is the name. The verse says, “…because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them.” (Esther 9:3) The next verse adds that he exercised great power in the palace and his fame spread through the provinces. A name that travels that far, I can only dream about. My name spread as far as the end of one counter.

Esther is the queen, and she's right in the middle of this story. But this verse names a different person: the fear of Mordecai had fallen on the officials (Esther 9:3). Mordecai, her cousin, is the one with the great power in the palace (Esther 9:4).

Xerxes is the king of Persia, and the provinces belong to him. But the verse names someone else as the one whose fear had fallen on the officials: Mordecai (Esther 9:3). The king gets the crown, and Mordecai gets the fame in this verse.

Five hundred is the number. The text says, “In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men,” (Esther 9:6). I think this is one of the heavier numbers in the story, so let's just let it be a heavy number. It's the count the king hears about later (Esther 9:12).
Two hundred isn't the number the verse gives. It says five hundred men in the citadel of Susa (Esther 9:6). I think this is a heavy line, and it's worth getting the number right.
That's more than the text says. In the citadel of Susa, the number is five hundred men (Esther 9:6). I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story, so I'd rather keep it exactly as written.

True, and it's worth noticing. The text says the Jews killed Haman's ten sons, “but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” (Esther 9:10) Haman, son of Hammedatha, was the man who had plotted against the Jews. The king's letter had allowed plunder (Esther 8:11), and the text says they didn't take it.

The text says the opposite. Right after naming Haman's ten sons, it says, “…they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” (Esther 9:10) The king's letter allowed plunder (Esther 8:11), so they could have. The verse says only that they didn't.

That's the one. King Xerxes says, “Now what is your petition? It will be given to you.” (Esther 9:12) He asked her the same sort of thing before (Esther 5:6; 7:2). I like a king who keeps the door open. I only had a drawer.

The king doesn't ask about Mordecai here. His question to Queen Esther is about her request: “Now what is your petition?” (Esther 9:12) He also asks what the Jews did in the rest of the provinces. It's the same kind of question he asked her earlier (Esther 5:6; 7:2).

That's not what he asks. After telling her the count from Susa, he asks, “Now what is your petition? It will be given to you.” (Esther 9:12) He'd asked her something like that before (Esther 5:6; 7:2). This time it comes with a promise attached.

Tomorrow it is. Esther says, “…may the Jews in Susa also have tomorrow to carry out today's edict…” (Esther 9:13). She asks for one more day, nothing longer. That's the kind of ask you make when you're counting on a short list.

A week is way more than she asks for. Esther's words are “…may the Jews in Susa also have tomorrow to carry out today's edict…” (Esther 9:13). One day, baker. I've asked for a week to finish a batch, and I'm no queen.
A month would be a lot to ask, and she doesn't. Esther asks that the Jews in Susa also have “tomorrow” to carry out today's edict (Esther 9:13). The request is just one extra day.

Not this time. The text says, “So the king commanded that this be done.” (Esther 9:14) He had told her whatever she asked would be given (Esther 9:12), and he did what he said. No turning down, friend.

That's right, it's false. “So the king commanded that this be done.” (Esther 9:14) An edict was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman. He said her requests would be fulfilled (Esther 9:12), and that's what happened.

Three hundred is the number. The text says the Jews in Susa came together again and “put to death three hundred men there” (Esther 9:15). It's a heavy count, and I'll leave it as the text gives it. The verse also says they didn't lay a hand on the plunder.
That's higher than the text says. On the fourteenth, the Jews in Susa put to death three hundred men (Esther 9:15). I think it's a heavy part of the story, so I want the number exactly right.
That's lower than what the text says. The count for the fourteenth in Susa is three hundred men (Esther 9:15). This is a heavy part of the story, and I'd rather give you the number as written.

Right, the text says, “They killed 75,000 who hated them, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” (Esther 9:16) That's a big number, and a heavy one. I think it's best to let it stand as the count the text gives. And again, the plunder stays untouched.
That's lower than the text says. The count in the royal provinces is 75,000 who hated them (Esther 9:16). It's a heavy number, so I'd rather you get the real one.
That's higher than the text gives. In the royal provinces, the number is 75,000 (Esther 9:16). It's a heavy part of the story, and I'd rather keep it as written.

True! The verse says, “…on the fourteenth day they rested, making it a day of feasting and joy.” (Esther 9:17) After a heavy stretch, the day ends in rest. I'll take a day of rest and feasting any time, as long as nobody asks me to clean the oven.
The text says otherwise. “…on the fourteenth day they rested, making it a day of feasting and joy.” (Esther 9:17) The Jews in the provinces took that day to rest. So it's rest, feasting and joy.

The fifteenth. The Jews in Susa assembled on the thirteenth and the fourteenth, “So they rested on the fifteenth day, making it a day of feasting and joy.” (Esther 9:18) They got their rest one day later than the provinces did. Same joy, different day on the calendar.
The fourteenth is when the Jews in the provinces rested (Esther 9:17). The Jews in Susa were still gathering that day. So the text says they rested on the fifteenth (Esther 9:18).
That's one day too late. The text says the Jews in Susa assembled on the thirteenth and fourteenth, “So they rested on the fifteenth day…” (Esther 9:18). Fifteenth, not sixteenth, baker.
That's it. The verse calls it “…a holiday for sending gifts to one another.” (Esther 9:19) I'm a big fan of any holiday where gifts go around. Nobody in that line is left holding an empty box.

Foot washing is something Jesus did with His disciples (John 13:5), but it's not what this holiday is. Here, the verse says it's “…a holiday for sending gifts to one another.” (Esther 9:19) So this one is about gifts.

explanations.answer: Read the Law to one another
explanations.explanation: That's not what this verse says. The fourteenth of Adar is a day of joy and feasting, “…a holiday for sending gifts to one another.” (Esther 9:19) Reading the Law doesn't appear in this verse. It's gifts, friend.
